rows: Chainsaws can cause fatal or major injuries when used incorrectly.
People using chainsaws at work require training relevant to the work they perform.
Operators should be competent for the specific chainsaw task.
Chainsaws should be selected and maintained for the intended work.
Appropriate chainsaw protective clothing should be provided and worn.
Work planning should address lone working, first aid and emergency arrangements.
Tree felling and off-ground chainsaw work require task-specific controls.
Operators should not bypass good practice to save time.
A chainsaw certificate or PPE list does not prove a particular cut or felling operation is safe.
Task conclusions require tree or material, saw, maintenance, competence, position, PPE, exclusion and emergency evidence.
Arboricultural lifting operations should be properly planned, supervised and carried out safely.
Ropes, harnesses, rigging systems, MEWPs and cranes can fall within lifting-equipment duties.
Lifting equipment should be suitable and strong enough for the intended load.
Anchor points form part of the lifting system and require competent selection.
Equipment used to lift people requires controls appropriate to that higher consequence.
Pre-use checks and thorough examinations should be completed by competent people as applicable.
Loads should be controlled to prevent free fall, drift or contact with people.
Reliable rescue arrangements should be available for aerial work.
A rope inspection record or safe-working-load mark does not prove a rigging operation is safe.
Operation conclusions require tree condition, anchors, equipment, examination, load, positioning, competence and rescue evidence.
Quad bikes and ATVs can rapidly become unstable on unsuitable terrain or when poorly loaded.
Quad-bike riders should wear suitable head protection.
Quad bikes are generally intended for a single operator rather than passengers.
Operators should receive adequate training for the vehicle and task.
Tyres, brakes, throttle and other safety-critical components require checks and maintenance.
Loads should be secured, balanced and within the vehicle's limits.
Routes should be planned and unfamiliar terrain checked for hidden hazards.
Side-by-side vehicles should use rollover protection and seat restraints where specified.
A vehicle model or training record does not prove safe use on a particular route.
Use conclusions require terrain, slope, weather, load, attachments, vehicle condition, operator and route evidence.
Handling cattle and other livestock can cause serious injury.
Work with livestock should be risk assessed and controlled.
Handling facilities should be suitable and maintained in good condition.
Races and crushes should match the animals and tasks.
Workers should be trained and competent in animal handling.
Temperamental or aggressive animals require appropriate management and culling decisions.
Visitors such as veterinary staff should be protected by the handling arrangements.
Equipment and escape routes should reduce the chance of crushing or trapping.
Animal breed or facility presence does not prove a handling task is safe.
Task conclusions require animal behaviour, group, facilities, equipment, worker position, competence and escape evidence.
